slides.label: The first conversation.
slides.notes: Open cold. Read the finish line and leave it up: today ends with a real call in a breakout room and an appointment inside it.
slides.html:
Zillow Preferred Onboarding · Day 2

The first conversation.

You get about five minutes. The buyer already decided what they want from an agent before you dialed. Today is about being that.

Today's finish line

You run a full call in a breakout room, and you set an appointment in it.

Not a perfect call. A real one.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 01 / 31

slides.label: Before anything else — a question for the room.
slides.notes: Do not answer it yourself. Wait through the silence, take three or four answers, and keep them where the room can see. You come back to this list two slides from now.
slides.html:
Before anything else — a question for the room.

Somebody clicks a house on Zillow and you call them. Take thirty seconds and answer this honestly.

Stop and talk

When that buyer picks up the phone, what are they actually deciding about you?

Say it out loud. We will come back to your answers in a minute.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 02 / 31

slides.label: They are asking one question.
slides.notes: Read the left column, then the right. The gap between them is the entire day. Land the closing paragraph slowly — right now they just want to see a house.
slides.html:
The one question

They are asking one question.

"Who is going to open the door for me?" That is most of it.

What we think they weigh
Years in the business
Market knowledge
Credentials and awards
How hard we negotiate
What they actually weigh
Who will open the door
Who makes this easy
Who answers fastest
Who puts the fewest things in the way

They have not thought the details through yet. Financing, timelines, neighborhoods, what they can really afford — none of that is resolved in their head. Right now they want to see a house.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 03 / 31

slides.label: Quick round — the worst sales call you have ever gotten.
slides.notes: Keep this list — it is the next slide. Let the room vent for a minute; everybody has a story, and that is the point.
slides.html:
Quick round — the worst sales call you have ever gotten.

Not real estate. Any call, any industry. The one that made you want to hang up.

Stop and talk

What did they do that made you want to get off the phone?

Drop it in the chat. We are keeping this list — it comes back on the next slide. Everybody has one. That is the point.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 04 / 31

slides.label: The fastest way to lose an online lead.
slides.notes: Say both lines out loud in a normal agent voice. Then point at the list the room just built — most of it is on this slide, and most of it is us.
slides.html:
The pattern

The fastest way to lose an online lead.

Look back at the list you just made. Most of it is on this slide — and most of it is us.

What it sounds like

"They're not serious unless they're pre-approved."

Or this

"It's not worth my time until they answer my questions."

That is a gatekeeper deciding who deserves service. The buyer feels it inside thirty seconds. Then they go and find somebody who does not make them audition first — and that person gets the appointment, the showing, and the sale.

Screening people before you serve them is the single biggest reason agents fail on online leads.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 05 / 31

slides.label: Advocate, not gatekeeper.
slides.notes: Callback to Day 1. Read the two columns as a pair, line by line. The test at the bottom is the thing to remember: every recommendation traces back to something they said.
slides.html:
The stance

Advocate, not gatekeeper.

Day 1 said an advisor puts the customer first and solves the real problem. This is what that sounds like on the phone.

A gatekeeper
Screens before serving
Asks about money first
Uses questions to qualify you
Sells urgency nobody asked for
An advocate
Serves, then learns
Asks what you want to see
Uses questions to understand you
Recommends from what you actually said

The test — every recommendation should trace back to something the buyer actually said.

A pitch

"Buy now — prices are going up."

Advice

"You said three bedrooms by spring. Here are two."

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 06 / 31

slides.label: Before you dial — ten minutes.
slides.notes: Ten minutes, and the three exceptions. If they asked for a text, text them — then work toward the call.
slides.html:
Speed to lead

Before you dial — ten minutes.

How fast you call is the first thing the buyer ever experiences from you. It is also the easiest thing on this list to get right.

10
minutes

from accepting the lead to the phone ringing

Unless
It is a live transfer — you are already talking.
The call is already scheduled for a set time.
They asked to be texted first.

If they asked for a text, text them — and work toward a call. A thread hides everything you need. Text to earn the call, then have the conversation.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 07 / 31

slides.label: The whole call is about five minutes.
slides.notes: Five minutes is permission, not a limit. Keeping somebody on the phone is a barrier too — get what you need, book the time, let them go.
slides.html:
Call length

The whole call is about five minutes.

Most first calls run under five minutes. Very few go past ten.

What five minutes buys you
An appointment on the calendar
A few facts you did not have
A reason for them to meet you
What it rules out
A full interview
A financing conversation
Twenty questions about their life

Keeping somebody on the phone is a barrier too. Get what you need, book the time, let them go.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 08 / 31

slides.label: Before we go on — when do you ask for the appointment?
slides.notes: One answer each, in the chat. Most of the room will say 'once they seem serious' — that is the belief the next slide takes apart.
slides.html:
Before we go on — when do you ask for the appointment?

Think about your last ten calls, not the ideal version of you.

Stop and talk

At what point in the call do you actually ask to go show them the home?

Beginning, middle, end, or only once they seem serious? One answer in the chat. Most of us have been taught to earn it first.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 09 / 31

slides.label: Four beats. That is the whole call.
slides.notes: Just the shape for now — they drill each beat later. The order is the lesson: the appointment ask comes before discovery.
slides.html:
The spine of the call

Four beats. That is the whole call.

You will drill each one separately in a few minutes. For now, just see the shape.

L Lead with who you are Name, brokerage, Zillow, and why you are calling.
E Extend the invitation Ask for the appointment. Give them this or that.
A Ask and listen Permission first, then a handful of questions.
D Deliver the summary Give the call back to them and confirm what is next.

In that order. The appointment ask comes before discovery, not after it.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 10 / 31

slides.label: Lead with who you are.
slides.notes: Ten seconds, four elements. Have two or three people say the example out loud before moving on.
slides.html:
Beat one · L

Lead with who you are.

Four things, in about ten seconds. Say them the same way every time until you stop having to think about it.

1

Your name

2

Your brokerage and your team

3

That you are partnered with Zillow

4

Why you are calling — the property they were looking at

What it sounds like

"Hi, this is Sam with Northside Realty — we're a featured partner with Zillow. I saw you were looking at 1234 Lane Street."

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 11 / 31

slides.label: Extend the invitation.
slides.notes: The counterintuitive one: ask before discovery. They raised their hand — you are offering the exact thing they came for. Two options, never yes-or-no.
slides.html:
Beat two · E

Extend the invitation.

Ask for the appointment now, before you ask them a single thing about themselves.

The ask

"Out of curiosity, when were you looking to go see it — do mornings or afternoons usually work better for you?"

Why this is not the leap it feels like

These buyers picked the house themselves — a tour request or connection means they raised their hand. You are not pushing anything on them; you are offering the exact thing they came for.

Two options, never yes-or-no

"Do you want to see it?" invites a no. "Mornings or afternoons?" invites a choice. Same question — completely different odds.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 12 / 31

slides.label: Ask and listen.
slides.notes: Permission first, always. Then open book vs closed book, and layering. The probe about other homes tells you if another agent is already in the picture.
slides.html:
Beat three · A

Ask and listen.

Permission first. Then a handful of questions — not an interview.

Ask permission before you ask anything else

"It sounds like we're seeing the home at five. Do you have a couple of minutes? I want to get the questions out of the way so I can take care of you properly."

Open book

Talks freely. Spend the time building rapport.

Closed book

Gives you very little. Work on motivation — why now, why here.

Layering

Buyer: "I really like the backyard." Weak: "Cool." Better: "You like the backyard? Do you entertain? Do you have kids?"

One probe worth having in your pocket: "Have you had a chance to go see any other homes?" It tells you whether somebody else is already helping them — without asking them to justify anything.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 13 / 31

slides.label: Quick one — would you stay in that store?
slides.notes: Let it land. Nobody stays. Hold that feeling into the next slide — it is exactly what a money question does on a first call.
slides.html:
Quick one — would you stay in that store?

You walk into a shop to look at something. Before anybody shows you anything, an employee comes over and asks you this.

Stop and talk

"Before we go any further — can you actually afford to shop here?"

Do you stay and answer? Or do you turn around and walk out? Nobody stays. Hold that feeling for the next slide.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 14 / 31

slides.label: What you do not ask on a first call.
slides.notes: The three questions you do not ask, and why. Financing is Day 4, after the appointment — not never.
slides.html:
The line

What you do not ask on a first call.

This is the clearest line there is between an advocate and a gatekeeper.

"Are you pre-approved?"

"What's your budget?"

"How much are you putting down?"

None of that is yours yet.

You have not met them. Asking makes a stranger justify themselves to you before you have done anything for them — exactly the barrier they were screening for. Financing is Day 4, once there is a relationship to have that conversation inside of. You are not avoiding the subject forever — you are putting it after the appointment instead of in front of it.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 15 / 31

slides.label: Deliver the summary.
slides.notes: Three parts, then the example. They hear that you were listening, and you both hang up with the same understanding of what happens next.
slides.html:
Beat four · D

Deliver the summary.

End every call by giving it back to them.

1 What we talked about Say it back in one sentence.
2 What you are looking for Their words, not your interpretation.
3 What happens next, and when A time, a date, and who does what.
What it sounds like

"So — Saturday at eleven, 1234 Lane Street. You're after three bedrooms, close to the east side, hoping to be in by spring. I'll text you the address tonight and confirm Friday."

They hear that you were actually listening — and you both hang up with the same understanding of what happens next, which is the thing that stops leads going quiet.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 16 / 31

slides.label: What they actually say.
slides.notes: Three openers, only one is really an objection. Notice what none of these are: no.
slides.html:
Objection handling

What they actually say.

Three openers cover most first calls. Only one of them is really an objection at all.

Questions about the property

"So tell me about the house..."

The most common by a mile — interest, not resistance. The one worth having a plan for.

Who am I talking to

"Are you the listing agent?"

"I actually work with the listing agent — I just happen to represent the buyer." True, disarming, and it moves right on.

Not ready yet

"I am just looking."

Almost always bundled with questions about the house. Treat it the same way.

Notice what none of these are: no. They are all openings.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 17 / 31

slides.label: Six moves. The fourth one is the whole thing.
slides.notes: Walk the six slowly. The fourth is the whole thing — park, do not answer. Most agents blow the call at move four.
slides.html:
The response

Six moves. The fourth one is the whole thing.

What to do the moment the questions start.

1 Acknowledge "No worries at all. What questions do you have?"
2 Capture Write every one of them down. All of them.
3 Clarify Ask about the questions if you need to. Do not answer them.
4 Park Say you will get them addressed — then stop. Do not answer.
5 Get permission "Real quick, I had a couple of questions for you. Is that okay?"
6 Go to discovery Motivation, location, timing. The A beat.
TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 18 / 31

slides.label: Then bring them back at the end.
slides.notes: The honest reason, then the natural delivery. A room can hear recitation instantly.
slides.html:
Closing the loop

Then bring them back at the end.

The honest reason

Photos online do not always match the house. Getting every question answered and then finding that out is a wasted trip for them. So you answer the questions and see the house in one go.

Six moves, not a script

Learn the six moves and the reason at the middle of them, then say it however you actually talk. A room can hear recitation instantly — and the second it sounds rehearsed you have lost the pressure-free tone.

How it comes out

"Let me do this — I'll get the answers to all of these, bring them with me, and we'll look at the house at the same time. Two birds, one trip. So are you open to going and taking a look?"

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 19 / 31

slides.label: When the home is already under contract.
slides.notes: Under contract: run the call as normal, use the confirm window to find matches, call back with good news or bad news first.
slides.html:
The edge case

When the home is already under contract.

You know it. They do not. Leading with it ends the call, and they walk away with nothing.

1 Run the call as normal. Gather what they are actually looking for.
2 Close by confirming the time: "I will reach out to the sellers and confirm."
3 Use that window — go find homes that match what they told you.
4 Call back with a choice: "Good news or bad news first?"
The callback

"The bad news is that home is still under contract — I will still try to get you in to see it. The good news is I found a few very similar ones. And since we were meeting at five anyway, I figured we would look at those too. Does that sound alright?"

You keep the appointment, and they get more than they asked for. That is the difference between an advocate and somebody who just delivers bad news.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 20 / 31

slides.label: Now you talk.
slides.notes: Divider into the practice block. Pairs, a few minutes each. You will be bad at it the first time — that is why we do it here.
slides.html:
Part two

Now you talk.

Three drills. One beat at a time. Nobody runs a whole call yet.

How this goes

Pairs. A few minutes each. You will be bad at it the first time — that is exactly why we do it here instead of on a real buyer.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 21 / 31

slides.label: Drill 1 — the introduction.
slides.notes: Timebox: five minutes total. Listen for anyone dropping one of the four elements.
slides.html:
Drill 1 of 3 · Breakout rooms

Drill 1 — the introduction.

Ten seconds, four elements, said out loud until it stops feeling strange.

In your breakout room
Pairs. Partner A goes first.
Say your whole introduction out loud. All four elements.
Do it three times. Change nothing but your delivery.
Swap. Partner B does the same.
Five minutes total.
Bring back

One thing that felt awkward coming out of your mouth.

Reminder

Your name · your brokerage and team · partnered with Zillow · the property they were looking at.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 22 / 31

slides.label: Drill 2 — the appointment ask.
slides.notes: Three versions of the ask; the listener says yes once, deflects once, asks a question once.
slides.html:
Drill 2 of 3 · Breakout rooms

Drill 2 — the appointment ask.

Three versions of the same ask. Always two options, never yes-or-no.

In your breakout room
Pairs. Partner B goes first this time.
Ask for the appointment three different ways.
Whoever is listening: say yes once, deflect once, ask a question once.
Swap. Partner A does the same.
Five minutes total.
Bring back

The version that felt most natural when you said it.

Reminder

"When were you looking to go see it — do mornings or afternoons usually work better?"

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 23 / 31

slides.label: Drill 3 — parking the questions.
slides.notes: The hard one — the agent may not answer either question. Moves 1 through 5 only.
slides.html:
Drill 3 of 3 · Breakout rooms

Drill 3 — parking the questions.

The hard one. You are not allowed to answer anything.

In your breakout room
Pairs. Partner A is the agent.
Partner B opens with two questions about the house. Any two.
The agent runs moves 1 through 5 — and may not answer either question.
Swap. Partner B is the agent.
Six minutes total.
Bring back

How hard it was not to answer, and what you said instead.

Reminder

Acknowledge · capture · clarify · park · get permission. Then discovery.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 24 / 31

slides.label: Now the whole call, start to finish.
slides.notes: Rooms of two, fifteen minutes. The agent does not read the buyer's scenario — that is deliberate. Buyers play it straight.
slides.html:
The full run

Now the whole call, start to finish.

Four beats, five minutes, one buyer who is not going to make it easy.

In your breakout room
Rooms of two. Partner A is the agent, Partner B plays Buyer 1 from their own workbook.
Five minutes. Run all four beats — L, E, A, D.
Then two minutes: the buyer says what landed and what did not.
Swap roles. Come back in fifteen minutes.
You do not get to read your buyer's scenario.

That is deliberate — what they want is something you have to find, the same way you would on a real call.

Buyers — play it straight.

Do not be deliberately difficult and do not hand everything over. Answer the way your card says you would.

The goal is an appointment. If you get one in the first minute, keep going — you still owe them A and D.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 25 / 31

slides.label: Back together — what happened?
slides.notes: Take a few stories per question, not all of them. Number four is the one they write down before leaving.
slides.html:
Debrief

Back together — what happened?

1 Who got an appointment? What did you say right before they agreed to it?
2 Who got stuck? Where exactly did it come apart — which beat?
3 Buyers — what did your agent miss? What were you ready to tell them that they never asked for?
4 What will you change? One thing, on your very next real call.

Write your answer to number four down before you leave this session.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 26 / 31

slides.label: Most of them will not pick up.
slides.notes: L and E with nobody on the other end. No discovery — there is nobody to discover. Direct beats clever.
slides.html:
When they don't pick up

Most of them will not pick up.

The voicemail is not a new script. It is L and E, with nobody on the other end.

The voicemail

"Hey, my name is Sam. I'm with Northside Realty, and we're featured partners with Zillow. It looks like you were interested in seeing — or had some questions about — 1234 Lane Street. I have some times open this afternoon and some in the morning. Let me know when you're free to talk so I can get you taken care of."

Nothing new to learn — the same four elements, the same this-or-that ask.

No discovery — there is nobody to discover. That is the whole trick.

Direct beats clever. Say who you are, say why you called, and give them two times.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 27 / 31

slides.label: Then text them.
slides.notes: Text supports the call, it does not replace it. If they answer by text, the next move is still to get them on the phone.
slides.html:
Follow-up

Then text them.

The first text

"Hi Jordan — Sam with Northside Realty, featured partner with Zillow. Just left you a voicemail about 1234 Lane Street. I have time this afternoon or tomorrow morning — which works better for you?"

Calls carry this. Text supports it.

Text is how you get a conversation, not how you have one. If they answer by text, your next move is still to get them on the phone. A thread cannot carry a real conversation — you cannot hear how somebody says a thing, and a sentence that reads flat on a screen gets taken completely the wrong way. Answer their text, be useful, and move it to a call.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 28 / 31

slides.label: How many times do you follow up before you stop?
slides.notes: No judgment — get the honest number in the chat before showing the next slide.
slides.html:
Stop and talk

How many times do you follow up before you stop?

One? Two? Three, and then it quietly falls off the list?

Not what you know you are supposed to do — what you actually do. One number in the chat. No judgment.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 29 / 31

slides.label: The first seven days do the work.
slides.notes: Front-load the effort. After week one the odds drop sharply. Every attempt is a note and a dated task — the framework only works if the record is true.
slides.html:
Persistence

The first seven days do the work.

When you cannot reach somebody, this is where the effort goes — and where it stops paying.

5–7

attempts across the first week

Front-load it

Most of your attempts belong in the first few days, not spread thin across a month.

Lead with calls

Text around them. The call is the instrument; the text is support.

After week one

The odds drop off sharply. Effort spent late is mostly effort wasted.

Every one of those attempts is a note and a dated task. A call with no note is a call nobody can see. The framework only works if the record behind it is true.

TRU · Zillow Preferred OnboardingDay 2 · 30 / 31

slides.label: Your own words, not mine.
slides.notes: Close on the homework — their own words, one real lead this week, note and dated task behind them. Tee up Day 3: the showing.
slides.html:
Before Day 3

Your own words, not mine.

Nobody sounds good reciting somebody else's script. The four beats are fixed. The words are yours.

Your homework

Write your own version of each of the four beats. Then run it on one real lead this week — and leave the note and the dated task behind you.
